name: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
aliases: Vitamin D metabolism and bone remodeling

clinicalPearls: Bone is continuously remodeled by a basic multicellular unit: osteoblasts (mesenchymal origin) lay down and mineralize osteoid, osteoclasts (hematopoietic/macrophage lineage) resorb matrix, and long-lived embedded osteocytes coordinate both and act as mechanosensors (Harrison 22e p.3259).

Roughly half of total serum calcium is ionized; the rest is bound to albumin/immunoglobulins or complexed to anions, so total calcium must be interpreted with the serum protein level. A useful correction adds about 0.8 mg/dL to total calcium for each 1 g/dL the albumin is below normal, but in acute illness measure ionized calcium directly with a calcium-selective electrode (Harrison 22e p.3261-3262).
Acidosis raises ionized calcium by reducing calcium binding to protein; alkalosis does the opposite, which helps explain tetany seen with respiratory alkalosis (Harrison 22e p.3262).

Serum phosphate varies by up to 50% over a day with a morning nadir, and IV dextrose, insulin, or alkalosis can drop it acutely, so phosphate should be measured fasting and in the basal state (Harrison 22e p.3262-3263).
Because only about 1% of body magnesium is in the extracellular fluid, a normal serum magnesium does not exclude significant total-body magnesium depletion (Harrison 22e p.3266-3267).

Hypomagnesemia frequently causes refractory hypocalcemia and hypokalemia; at very low serum magnesium (below roughly 0.4 mmol/L) PTH secretion is impaired and there is cellular PTH resistance, so calcium and potassium will not correct until magnesium is repleted (Harrison 22e p.3267).

FGF23, secreted by osteocytes, is a phosphaturic hormone that both lowers proximal-tubule phosphate reabsorption and suppresses 1-alpha-hydroxylase (lowering 1,25(OH)2D); excess FGF23 underlies XLH, ADHR, and tumor-induced osteomalacia, whereas deficient/inactive FGF23 causes tumoral calcinosis (Harrison 22e p.3263-3265).

Vitamin D is effectively a hormone, not a true vitamin: skin synthesizes it from 7-dehydrocholesterol under UV light, the liver performs unregulated 25-hydroxylation (25(OH)D is the storage/measured form), and the kidney performs the tightly regulated 1-alpha-hydroxylation to active 1,25(OH)2D (Harrison 22e p.3268).

Renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase is stimulated by PTH and hypophosphatemia and suppressed by calcium, FGF23, and 1,25(OH)2D itself; granuloma/lymphoma macrophages express an unregulated 1-alpha-hydroxylase, explaining hypercalcemia in sarcoidosis and lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.3268).

Optimal intestinal calcium absorption requires gastric acid; achlorhydria, proton pump inhibitors, or post-bariatric surgery impair absorption of poorly dissociable salts like calcium carbonate, so calcium citrate or dosing with meals is preferred (Harrison 22e p.3262).

Active vitamin D-dependent transcellular calcium and phosphate absorption uses specific apical channels/transporters (TRPV6 and Npt2b in the gut, TRPV5 in the distal tubule); thiazides lower urinary calcium (useful in hypercalciuria) while loop diuretics and saline promote calciuresis (Harrison 22e p.3262).

Serious neuromuscular sequelae of hypophosphatemia (seizures, paralysis, rhabdomyolysis) occur mainly when phosphate falls below about 0.25 mmol/L, reflecting ATP depletion; up to 30% of patients with acute hypophosphatemia have CPK elevations peaking 1-2 days after the phosphate nadir (Harrison 22e p.3264).
harrison.pathophysiology: Mineral homeostasis is maintained by integrated handling of calcium, phosphate, and magnesium across gut, kidney, and bone under hormonal control by PTH, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, and FGF23. Bone provides both mechanical support and the major reservoir of these ions; it is constantly remodeled, with osteoblasts (mesenchymal lineage, driven by Runx2, osterix, Ihh, Wnt and BMP signaling) forming and mineralizing type I collagen matrix and osteoclasts (hematopoietic lineage, driven by M-CSF and RANK ligand, opposed by osteoprotegerin) resorbing it via acidification and proteases such as cathepsin K. Osteocytes sense mechanical load, secrete the Wnt inhibitor sclerostin and the phosphaturic hormone FGF23, and orchestrate remodeling. Ionized calcium in the extracellular fluid is sensed by the calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid cells and renal tubule; low calcium raises PTH, which mobilizes bone calcium, enhances distal renal calcium reabsorption, lowers renal phosphate reabsorption, and stimulates renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase to make 1,25(OH)2D, which in turn increases intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption. Phosphate balance is governed largely by proximal tubular NaPi-2a/2c transporters, which are downregulated by PTH and FGF23; FGF23 from osteocytes additionally suppresses 1,25(OH)2D synthesis. Vitamin D is produced in skin or absorbed from diet, 25-hydroxylated in liver, and 1-alpha-hydroxylated in kidney, with 24-hydroxylase (CYP24A1) providing inactivation. Disturbances at any node (dietary extremes, renal failure, hormone deficiency/excess, intestinal disease, or genetic transporter/enzyme defects) disrupt the narrow regulation of ionized calcium and lead to skeletal and systemic disease.
additionalDifferentials: Hypophosphatemia: primary/secondary hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, FGF23 excess (XLH, ADHR, ARHP, tumor-induced osteomalacia, McCune-Albright/fibrous dysplasia), Fanconi syndrome, Dent disease, alcoholism, poorly controlled diabetes, refeeding/insulin therapy, hungry bone syndrome
Hyperphosphatemia: renal insufficiency, hypoparathyroidism/pseudohypoparathyroidism, acromegaly, tumoral calcinosis, tumor lysis syndrome, rhabdomyolysis/crush injury, exogenous phosphate loads

Hypomagnesemia: malabsorption, proton pump inhibitor use, alcoholism, Gitelman and Bartter syndromes, claudin 16/19 mutations, TRPM6 mutation, drug-induced (cisplatin, aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, cyclosporine, cetuximab), diabetic glycosuria
Hypermagnesemia: renal failure with magnesium load, familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia, adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, eclampsia treatment
Hypercalcemia with elevated 1,25(OH)2D: sarcoidosis and other granulomatous disease, lymphoma, vitamin D intoxication, CYP24A1 inactivating mutation
Osteomalacia/rickets vs other causes of bone pain and proximal myopathy
infectionMimics: Granulomatous infections (e.g., tuberculosis, other mycobacterial or fungal granulomas) can drive macrophage 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity and produce 1,25(OH)2D-mediated hypercalcemia, mimicking non-infectious hypercalcemia
nonInfectiousMimics: Sarcoidosis and lymphoma as causes of 1,25(OH)2D-mediated hypercalcemia
Tumor-induced osteomalacia mimicking idiopathic chronic bone pain and myopathy
Milk-alkali syndrome mimicking other hypercalcemic states with renal impairment
additionalInvestigations: Serum total and ionized calcium (ionized preferred in acute illness), with albumin for correction
Fasting serum phosphate and serum magnesium
Intact PTH and PTHrP where malignancy-associated hypercalcemia is suspected
Serum FGF23 in unexplained hypophosphatemic osteomalacia or tumoral calcinosis
Fractional excretion of phosphate / renal phosphate threshold to confirm renal phosphate wasting
Bone formation markers (bone-specific alkaline phosphatase, osteocalcin, procollagen I N-terminal propeptide) and resorption markers (collagen cross-linked telopeptides in urine/blood)
Renal function (creatinine/GFR) given its central role in phosphate retention and vitamin D activation
Calcium-phosphorus product monitoring during phosphate repletion (avoid exceeding 50 mg2/dL2)
Imaging/localization for tumor-induced osteomalacia (skeletal survey, bone scan, octreotide or sestamibi scanning)
redFlags: Severe hypophosphatemia below about 0.25 mmol/L (0.8 mg/dL): risk of seizures, ascending paralysis, rhabdomyolysis, respiratory and cardiac failure, coma
Acute severe hyperphosphatemia: widespread calcium-phosphate precipitation with tetany, seizures, acute renal failure, and pulmonary/cardiac calcification including heart block
Hypermagnesemia above ~2 mmol/L: refractory hypotension, neuromuscular blockade, hyporeflexia progressing to respiratory failure, heart block, and asystole near 10 mmol/L
Severe hypomagnesemia: tetany, seizures, cardiac arrhythmias, prolonged QT and enhanced digitalis toxicity
Very high calcium intake or milk-alkali syndrome: hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis, progressive renal failure
harrison.prognosis: Prognosis depends entirely on the underlying disorder rather than on bone and mineral metabolism per se. Acute redistributive electrolyte derangements (hypophosphatemia, hypomagnesemia) are typically reversible with appropriate repletion, and respiratory/cardiac dysfunction from severe hypophosphatemia improves with phosphate replacement. Tumor-induced osteomalacia resolves within hours to days after successful tumor resection. Chronic renal phosphate-wasting disorders (XLH, ADHR) generally cannot be fully normalized but can be controlled. Persistent dysregulation, as in chronic kidney disease with secondary hyperparathyroidism and hyperphosphatemia, leads to progressive skeletal and vascular consequences.
pitfalls: Relying on total serum calcium without correcting for albumin, or on corrected calcium during acute illness, can mislead; ionized calcium should be measured directly when accuracy matters
A normal serum magnesium does not exclude total-body magnesium depletion because the extracellular pool is tiny
The body phosphate deficit cannot be predicted from a single serum phosphate; repletion must be empirical and monitored, since the nadir often occurs hours into insulin/glucose therapy

Giving IV magnesium alone to a patient with combined hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia, and hypophosphatemia can worsen hypophosphatemia by abruptly restoring PTH secretion; give calcium and magnesium together
Failing to recognize that hypocalcemia and hypokalemia are refractory until magnesium is repleted
Overlooking 1,25(OH)2D-mediated hypercalcemia from granulomatous disease or lymphoma, where calcium does not suppress the ectopic 1-alpha-hydroxylase
Phosphate measured non-fasting or after IV dextrose can be spuriously low; rapid phosphate correction risks heterotopic calcification if the calcium-phosphorus product is allowed to rise
harrison.severityClassification: Hypophosphatemia is graded by serum phosphate (mild-moderate ~0.5-0.8 mmol/L [1.5-2.5 mg/dL] with mainly musculoskeletal/reversible cardiorespiratory effects; severe <0.5 mmol/L [<1.5 mg/dL]; life-threatening <0.25 mmol/L [<0.8 mg/dL] with paralysis, seizures, rhabdomyolysis). Hyperphosphatemia in adults is defined as fasting phosphate >1.8 mmol/L (5.5 mg/dL). Hypomagnesemia is usually asymptomatic above ~0.5 mmol/L; defects in PTH secretion appear below ~0.4 mmol/L. Hypermagnesemia produces vasodilation/neuromuscular blockade above ~2 mmol/L, coma and hyporeflexia above ~4 mmol/L, and asystole near 10 mmol/L.
management: Treat the specific underlying disorder driving the mineral derangement, since prognosis depends on it rather than the electrolyte disturbance itself
Replete magnesium first in hypomagnesaemia, as hypocalcaemia and hypokalaemia remain refractory until magnesium is restored owing to impaired PTH secretion and PTH resistance
Correct hypocalcaemia with calcium and activated vitamin D (calcitriol), guided by ionised calcium in acutely ill patients
Manage phosphate disorders by replacing phosphate in symptomatic hypophosphataemia and using phosphate binders with dietary restriction in hyperphosphataemia
Restore vitamin D status with cholecalciferol or ergocalciferol, using activated vitamin D analogues where 1-alpha-hydroxylation is deficient
Treat hypercalcaemia at source with fluids, antiresorptive bisphosphonates or denosumab, and directed therapy for malignancy or hyperparathyroidism
Monitor calcium, phosphate, magnesium, PTH and vitamin D, and support bone with antiresorptive or anabolic agents where turnover is deranged
